passage: "Swati, stay back a minute?" "Did I do something wrong, Ma'am?" "No. The opposite. In class you explained why the river changes course better than anyone. Where did that come from?" "I just... see it. The water pushing on the soft bank." "But your written test has three lines." "I know." Swati looks at the floor. "I try. I write it again and again. It comes out wrong." "I believe you try. I've watched you." Urmila, the geography teacher, pulls a chair over. "Can I ask your parents to meet the counsellor about a screening? It checks how your brain handles reading and writing." "So I'm not lazy?" "Lazy people don't rewrite things again and again. And I won't ask you to read aloud without warning anymore. Deal?" "Deal."

qa.a: Swati may stop feeling lazy and start seeing that the ideas are strong while writing is hard.

subtype: Teacher noticing a gap between effort and results [Observer]
passage: My name is Gopika, and I've taught maths for eleven years. I still think about Parveen, from two batches ago. She was the most careful student I had. Neat margins, every step written. And yet her answers were wrong in strange ways: 36 became 63, a plus sign read as a minus. At first I wrote "careless" in red. I'm not proud of that. Then I sat beside her during a test and watched. She was not careless. She was checking every line, lips moving, and still the digits slid. I stopped using red for those slips. I asked her family about a screening, and I started marking her method separately from her final number. Her method marks were among the best in the class. She stood a little straighter after that.

qa.q: What did Gopika write in red at first?
qa.a: Careless.

qa.q: What does Gopika saying 'I'm not proud of that' show about how Gopika feels now?
qa.a: It shows regret; looking back, Gopika feels she misjudged Parveen's effort.

qa.q: What did Gopika change after watching Parveen during a test?
qa.a: Gopika stopped marking the slips in red, asked the family about a screening and marked Parveen's method separately.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when her method marks were among the best?
qa.a: She probably felt seen and proud, since her careful effort finally counted; she stood a little straighter.

grounding: A teacher sees careful effort with number errors, suggests screening and values the student's thinking, separating learning difference from lack of effort.

passage:
Teacher's note, Ganga, History, Class 9.
In Tuesday's discussion on the salt march, Nitin spoke for five minutes without notes, linking the march to prices in his own grandfather's village. It was the best answer anyone gave. Then I marked his written test: four lines per answer, many words misspelt, one answer left unfinished. He had clearly tried; there were rubbings-out all over. The mismatch was too big to be laziness.
I stopped calling on him to read the textbook aloud without warning; he now gets the passage a day earlier. I phoned his parents that evening and suggested a screening with the school counsellor. In my marking I now give separate credit for ideas. Next step: meet the counsellor on Monday.

qa.q: What topic did Nitin speak about for five minutes?
qa.a: He spoke about the salt march, linking it to prices in his grandfather's village.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel on seeing the gap between Nitin's discussion and written test?
qa.a: Ganga felt puzzled and concerned, sensing the mismatch was too big to be laziness.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that separated a learning difference from lack of effort?
qa.a: Ganga stopped surprise reading aloud, gave the passage early, suggested screening to his parents and gave separate credit for ideas.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel about getting the passage a day early?
qa.a: Nitin may feel relieved and less anxious, able to prepare instead of fearing being put on the spot.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing strong oral answers but weak written work, and responding with screening, no surprise reading aloud and credit for ideas.

passage:
Wednesday night, staff room diary.
Avni, Class 11, stays after every physics class to redo problems. Her working is careful and neat, but the final numbers keep going wrong: 36 becomes 63, a minus sign vanishes. Today a boy said, "She just doesn't try," and she went red. It isn't true. I've watched her try harder than anyone.
When she brought me her notebook, the students were still calling me "Ujjwal Sir" through the doorway, and I kept my voice low. I said, "Your method is right. Let's look at the numbers together." I will not ask her to solve at the board in front of everyone again. Tomorrow I'll speak to her parents about screening for a number difficulty, and I'll mark her method separately.

qa.q: What happens to 36 in Avni's working?
qa.a: 36 becomes 63.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal Sir feel when the boy said Avni doesn't try?
qa.a: He felt protective and frustrated, knowing he had watched her try harder than anyone.

qa.q: Which of Ujjwal Sir's plans treats this as a learning difference rather than laziness?
qa.a: Suggesting screening for a number difficulty to her parents, marking her method separately and not putting her on the spot at the board.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when the boy made his comment?
qa.a: Avni probably felt humiliated and hurt, going red because her real effort was being called laziness.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing careful effort with repeated number errors, and responding with screening, no on-the-spot tasks and credit for method.

subtype: Teacher noticing a gap between effort and results [Observer]
passage:
Gurleen Ma'am had taught in the Nabha government school for twelve years, and something about Disha puzzled her. In class discussion Disha explained the causes of the monsoon better than anyone. Yet her written test was half blank, the letters cramped, some words spelled three ways.
In the next reading round, Gurleen noticed Disha's shoulders creep up as her turn came closer. Her eyes went flat and far away.
Gurleen skipped her without comment. After class she said quietly, "Your answer about the winds today was excellent. Writing seems much harder than speaking for you. Would you be okay if I talked to your mother about a screening at the block resource centre?"
Disha hesitated, then nodded.
From then on, Gurleen let her answer some questions aloud in tests and never asked her to read aloud without warning.

qa.q: What did Disha explain better than anyone in class discussion?
qa.a: The causes of the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Gurleen Ma'am feeling as she compared Disha's speaking and writing?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and concerned, sensing the gap came from a learning difference rather than laziness.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen Ma'am's steps would help other teachers?
qa.a: Praising the ideas, suggesting a screening, allowing oral answers and not making the student read aloud on the spot separate a learning difference from lack of effort.

qa.q: What is it like for Disha as her reading turn comes closer?
qa.a: She feels tense and anxious, her shoulders creeping up, and seems to go somewhere far away to cope.

grounding: Gurleen Ma'am notices the gap between Disha's strong oral answers and weak written work, suggests screening, avoids reading aloud on the spot and values her ideas.
